title: Molloy
significance: The first volume of the trilogy Beckett wrote in French. The wandering Molloy's monologue and the report of Moran, who sets out to find him, are laid side by side in two parts, and as the second narrator comes to resemble the first, the distinction between pursuer and pursued breaks down.

title: Malone Dies
significance: An old man confined to bed invents stories while waiting to die, and is exhausted along with the characters he creates. The second volume of the trilogy, it foregrounds a structure in which narration makes stories and discards them at the same time.

title: Waiting for Godot
significance: A two-act play with no incident beyond two men waiting, on the same spot for two days, for someone who never comes. Published in French by Éditions de Minuit in 1952 and premiered at the Théâtre de Babylone in Paris in 1953, it changed the range of what postwar theater could address.

title: The Unnamable
significance: The final volume of the trilogy, in which neither character nor place remains — only a voice that cannot stop talking. Paragraph breaks disappear, and the closing passage becomes a single flow held together by commas alone.

title: Endgame
significance: A one-act play in which a master who cannot move, a servant who cannot leave, and parents living in trash bins all wait for the end in a single room. It compresses the waiting of Waiting for Godot into a narrower space and fewer words.

title: The Gift
significance: Set against Berlin émigré society, it overlays a young writer's development with the history of Russian literature — Nabokov's last and longest novel written in Russian. When it was serialized in an émigré journal in 1937–38, the editors dropped Chapter Four, on Chernyshevsky, and the complete Russian edition did not appear until 1952.

title: Speak, Memory
significance: A memoir that arranges a pre-revolutionary Russian childhood not in chronological order but as a set of recurring patterns. It first appeared in the United States in 1951 under the title Conclusive Evidence, then went through a Russian-language edition before reaching its final, expanded form in a 1966 revised edition.

title: Lolita
significance: Rejected by every American publisher, it first appeared in 1955 from Olympia Press in Paris, and became the center of controversy after the 1958 American edition. Its structure is such that the more beautiful the narrator's sentences, the more his acts are obscured, testing the reader's own reading.

title: Pnin
significance: An episodic novel about a Russian émigré professor who never manages to secure a lasting place at an American university. The losses of a figure drawn as comic to that point are overturned at the end, when the narrator's identity is revealed.

title: Pale Fire
significance: A novel made up of nothing but a 999-line poem and the commentary that hijacks it. As the annotator rereads the poem as the story of his own exiled kingdom, it becomes impossible to decide which side is the fiction.

title: The Stranger
significance: It records, in a first person that offers no explanation of emotion, how the fact that he did not cry at his mother's funeral becomes the central piece of evidence at his murder trial. Its sentences, strung together in the compound past tense, are repeatedly cited as an example of a stylistic device that enacts the narrator's disconnection from the world.

title: The Myth of Sisyphus
significance: It opens by positing suicide as the philosophical question that must be answered first, and defines the absurd as the mismatch between a human being who demands meaning and a world that stays silent. Presenting a life that endures the absurd without resolving it as its conclusion, it became a reference point for postwar absurdist literature.

title: Caligula
significance: A four-act play in which an emperor who, after his sister's death, begins demanding the impossible, pushes his own logic to its end and arrives at catastrophe. Written in the late 1930s, it was published in 1944 and premiered in Paris in 1945.

title: The Plague
significance: It narrates, in the form of a doctor's record, the period in which the Algerian city of Oran is sealed off by plague. By presenting the everyday diligence of people enduring the disaster as a collective response to the absurd, it marks the turning point from the individual absurd to the problem of solidarity.

title: The Rebel
significance: It traces, from Greek tragedy to twentieth-century totalitarianism, the process by which rebellion becomes institutionalized as revolution and comes to justify murder. The controversy surrounding this book led to his break with Sartre's circle.

title: The Fall
significance: A short novel that proceeds entirely as a monologue, spoken by a man in an Amsterdam bar to an unnamed listener. His confession turns into a device that judges the listener instead, and it became the last novel Camus completed in his lifetime.

title: In Our Time
significance: A story collection that binds the whole volume into a single structure by inserting short vignettes of war and bullfighting between the stories. It expands a 1924 Paris pamphlet that had collected only the vignettes, and the Nick Adams stories begin here.

title: The Sun Also Rises
significance: His first novel, recording in dialogue-driven form the drifting of characters moving between Paris and Pamplona after the First World War. Gertrude Stein's phrase 'a lost generation,' used as this novel's epigraph, spread widely from here.

title: A Farewell to Arms
significance: It places the relationship between an ambulance driver and a nurse on the Italian front within a chronicle of retreat and death. The passage in which the narrator says that abstract words like glory and honor collapse before concrete place names and unit numbers is repeatedly cited as a summary of postwar literature's attitude.

title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
significance: It depicts three days of an American who joins a mountain guerrilla band to blow up a bridge during the Spanish Civil War. It is the longest of Hemingway's novels, and because it records atrocities committed by both sides, it drew criticism from both left and right.

title: The Old Man and the Sea
significance: A short novel recording three days of an old man, who has gone eighty-four days without catching a fish, in his struggle with a marlin. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1953, and this work was named specifically in the citation for his 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature.

title: Down and Out in Paris and London
significance: His first book, recording his own experience as a dishwasher in a Paris hotel kitchen and in London's lodging houses for vagrants. It is also where Eric Blair first used the name George Orwell.

title: Homage to Catalonia
significance: A record of his experience as a POUM militiaman on the Aragon front and in the 1937 street fighting in Barcelona. Because it reported the purges within the Republican side, it was shunned by the British left at the time of publication.

title: Animal Farm
significance: It compresses into a fable the process by which, after the farm animals drive out their owner, the new rule comes to resemble the old. Because it targeted the Soviet Union, then a wartime ally, several publishers rejected it, and it did not appear until around the war's end.

title: Politics and the English Language
significance: It shows, through analysis of actual examples, how political language conceals facts behind stock phrases and euphemism, and proposes six rules for restoring the sentence. It appeared in the magazine Horizon in April 1946.

title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
significance: It describes how memory and language are managed in a state where the Party continually rewrites the record of the past. The appendix on Newspeak presents the novel's theory of language as a separate structure, and the vocabulary that emerged from it became a common language for talking about totalitarianism.

title: She Came to Stay
significance: Her first novel, translating into narrative the threat that another person's consciousness poses to the self, through a triangular relationship between a couple and the young woman they take in.

title: The Second Sex
significance: A study of woman's condition, published in two volumes by Gallimard in 1949. After reviewing in turn the ways biology, psychoanalysis, and history have explained woman, it narrates, at the level of lived experience, the process by which woman is constituted as the 'Other' in a society that takes man as its standard.

title: The Mandarins
significance: It narrates, alternating between two points of view, how a group of Paris intellectuals in the years just after the Liberation splits apart over the question of Soviet camps and the onset of the Cold War. It won the Prix Goncourt in 1954.

title: Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter
significance: It narrates twenty years in which the daughter of a Catholic bourgeois family departs from the set path of faith and marriage and turns toward philosophy. The first volume of a four-part memoir series.

title: The Coming of Age
significance: It examines old age from the perspectives of biology, history, and society, and treats the ways the old are socially excluded through the same analysis of othering as The Second Sex — a major late work.

title: Death Fugue
significance: A poem that arranges the killing in the camps into phrases that repeat and cross like the voices of a fugue. It first appeared in 1947 in a Romanian translation; the German original was printed in his 1948 debut collection The Sand from the Urns, published in Vienna, and it became widely read only after being reprinted in Poppy and Memory in 1952.

title: Poppy and Memory
significance: The collection that made Celan's name known in the German-speaking world. It includes Death Fugue, and its images of loss and memory are still written in relatively open sentences, in contrast with the compression of his later work.

title: Sprachgitter
significance: A collection whose title presents language as both a medium of communication and, at the same time, a grille or barrier. The shorter lines, fewer words, and wider blank space of his later style begin here.

title: The No-One's Rose
significance: A collection dedicated to the memory of Mandelstam, in which Jewish tradition and Eastern European place names come to the foreground. Celan's dialogue with the Russian poets he was translating takes place directly within the poems.

title: Breathturn
significance: The collection in which the late style, cut down to the level of the individual word, becomes established. A single poem can run to only a few lines, with newly coined compounds and blank space standing in for sentences.
